sources.title: Country Climate and Development Report: Ecuador
sources.temporal_coverage: Reports historical flood and shoreline impacts, recent policy processes, and modeled climate, poverty and adaptation outcomes to 2050.
sources.methodology: Climate scenarios, hazard models, sector analysis and poverty microsimulation.
sources.limitations: Some impact estimates are cited; model results depend on scenarios.

sources.title: Análisis de choques en Ecuador - 2026
sources.organization: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
sources.temporal_coverage: Intersectoral shock analysis published May 2026; describes security-related operational constraints during 2025 and current humanitarian needs.
sources.methodology: OCHA intersectoral analysis summarizes 2026 shock needs and access conditions.
sources.limitations: Only the official publication-page text was accessible; the linked PDF was not opened.

sources.title: Food security impacts of organized criminal violence in Ecuador
sources.organization: Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET)
sources.temporal_coverage: Special report published 29 May 2026; describes recent violence and projects food-security and weather conditions for June–December 2026.
sources.methodology: FEWS NET combines food-security and weather analysis.
sources.limitations: Forecast reflects May 2026 information; local outcomes may vary.

claims.locator: PDF p. 84 (printed p. 72), Appendix 5.3.1, coastal flood and erosion impacts
claims.paraphrase: Twenty of 24 recorded heavy-rain flood disasters since 1992 affected a coastal province; erosion was highest in El Oro, Esmeraldas and Guayas.
claims.limitations: Recorded events and erosion estimates are historical, not a local forecast.

claims.locator: PDF p. 16 (printed p. 5), executive summary, poverty and regional vulnerability
claims.paraphrase: Poor communities in Amazon and coastal regions face flood vulnerability; indigenous peoples are especially exposed. Dry/hot projections raise rural poverty more than urban poverty by 2050.
claims.scenario: Dry/hot versus wet/warm scenarios; poverty projections to 2050.
claims.limitations: Modeled aggregate results; no community-level projection.

claims.locator: PDF p. 30 (printed p. 19), section 2.1, protests, policy legitimacy and climate targets
claims.paraphrase: CCDR says October 2019 and June 2022 mass protests paralyzed Ecuador and forced policy reversals affecting climate targets, including fuel-subsidy removal.
claims.limitations: The report discusses policy legitimacy; it does not characterize protests as violent.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: It explicitly links protests to reversals affecting climate targets and civil action to restrictions on oil and mining plans.

claims.locator: PDF p. 35 (printed p. 24), section 3.2.1, regional agricultural adaptation priorities
claims.paraphrase: CCDR recommends water-scarcity adaptation in the Guayas River basin and targeted irrigation and support for small farmers; these are priorities, not delivered results.
claims.limitations: Recommendations do not establish implementation or measured capacity.

claims.locator: Official publication page, paragraph 2, intersectoral needs estimate and ten provinces
claims.paraphrase: OCHA estimates 1.91 million people need assistance in ten priority provinces, concentrated in high-severity areas with simultaneous deprivations.
claims.limitations: Intersectoral need estimate; it does not isolate climate-attributable need.

claims.locator: Official publication page, paragraph 3, protection and security conditions
claims.paraphrase: Armed violence and criminal territorial control drive displacement, threats, extortion and service restrictions in coastal Guayas, Esmeraldas, Los Ríos, urban corridors and border zones.
affected_groups: people exposed to threats and extortion
claims.limitations: The page describes concentration and impacts; it does not claim every listed place is equally affected.

claims.locator: Official publication page, paragraphs 3–4, climate impacts and shock interactions
claims.paraphrase: Climate disasters damage infrastructure, livelihoods and safe-water access in coastal and Amazon provinces with limited state presence; OCHA says shocks interact and reinforce overlapping deprivations.
claims.limitations: OCHA reports cumulative interaction, not an isolated causal chain for each deprivation.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: OCHA says violence, climate events and socioeconomic fragility interact and reinforce simultaneous service deprivations.

claims.locator: Official publication page, paragraphs 5–6, humanitarian access restrictions and response capacity
claims.paraphrase: Security conditions, armed actors, mobility barriers, road damage and isolation restricted 2025 operations, limiting assessment, monitoring and sustained assistance.
claims.limitations: This is an access constraint, not proof that a named climate-adaptation project stopped.

claims.locator: Report page, Key Messages and opening food-security outlook
claims.paraphrase: FEWS projects violence-driven food insecurity, compounded by weather, among poor informal workers, displaced people, migrants and coastal fishers.
claims.scenario: Most-likely food-security outlook for June–December 2026; published 29 May 2026.
claims.limitations: FEWS identifies violence as the primary driver and weather as a compounding factor.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The report says violence drives food insecurity while climate hazards may compound impacts.

claims.locator: Report page, assumptions for the most-likely scenario, June–December 2026
claims.paraphrase: El Niño may reduce coastal fish income; episodic heavy rain and floods may disrupt livelihoods, markets and services in Amazon river areas.
claims.scenario: FEWS NET outlook for May–December 2026, including expected El Niño conditions.

claims.locator: Report page, assumptions for the most-likely scenario and food-security outlook
claims.paraphrase: Above-average heat may reduce irrigated second-season yields, while poor agricultural laborers face reduced work and income opportunities in coastal provinces.
claims.limitations: Food-security assessment; it provides no farm-level yield estimate.

claims.locator: Report page, sections on food availability, market functioning and violence impacts
claims.paraphrase: National food supplies and most markets remain functional, but curfews, extortion and logistics costs restrict access and purchasing power, especially for poor and displaced households.
claims.limitations: Available supply does not ensure affordability or safe access.

search_audit.query: Ecuador climate vulnerability provinces coastal Amazon poverty flood erosion named localities primary CCDR report
search_audit.outcome: Opened the full WB CCDR and official OCHA publication page; located coastal flood/erosion risk, Guayaquil, named coastal provinces, Amazon risks and differentiated poor/indigenous exposure.

search_audit.query: Ecuador climate security conflict violence protests climate targets vulnerability official primary reports
search_audit.outcome: The CCDR explicitly links 2019/2022 mass protests to policy reversals affecting climate targets; OCHA and FEWS NET describe interacting climate, violence, deprivation and food-access pathways without claiming climate caused violence.

search_audit.query: Ecuador armed violence insecurity displacement restrictions humanitarian access climate adaptation response official report
search_audit.outcome: OCHA reports security, armed actors, mobility and road-isolation constraints limiting humanitarian assessment, monitoring and sustained implementation; no opened source tied this specifically to a named climate-adaptation project.

search_audit.query: Ecuador regional adaptation irrigation Guayas River basin small farmers resilience institutional response capacity
search_audit.outcome: The CCDR recommends basin- and producer-specific water and agricultural measures; OCHA reports existing humanitarian response capacity is insufficient relative to needs; FEWS NET describes functional food supplies and markets alongside access barriers.

gaps: ECU is absent from EXISTING_COUNTRIES.json and no countries/ECU baseline dossier was present; this is a new-country extraction, not an extension of an existing record.

No reviewed source establishes that climate change caused criminal violence in Ecuador. The OCHA and FEWS NET reports explicitly describe interacting or compounding shocks, while the CCDR documents social-protest effects on climate-policy implementation.

OCHA’s accessible publication-page text summarizes the shock analysis; its linked PDF was not opened. The official National Adaptation Plan returned HTTP 502, the Second NDC PDF exceeded reader limits, and the IMF report page returned HTTP 403.

Security restrictions are documented as constraints on humanitarian operations and market access; the reviewed sources do not identify a specific climate-adaptation project that was suspended by insecurity.
FEWS NET’s June–December 2026 projections were published in May 2026; they are dated outlook estimates, not observed outcomes or a current post-May update.
